results.title: I replaced my password manager, VPN, and antivirus with free tools and saved $300 a year
results.author: Afam Onyimadu
results.content:
I kind of trust my subscriptions and smoke alarms in the same way. Once I've set them up, I stop thinking about them and assume they're doing their job. However, when I got three renewal emails for 1Password, NordVPN, and McAfee, it made me pause and think about what I was actually paying for.
I realized I was paying for specific capabilities that I could handle differently for free. Since then, I've saved more than $300 and haven't missed the parts of these services I actually used because I found options that fit my setup.
Password manager subscriptions
KeePassXC put my vault back in my own hands
I used 1Password's $2.99-a-month Individual plan ($35.88 a year) until April, when I canceled and switched to KeePassXC. I thought of the subscription as paying for password security, but when I broke it down, I was really paying for four different things: somewhere to store the vault, syncing across my phone and laptop, autofill, and breach alerts for my credentials.
KeePassXC approaches password storage differently. There isn't a company holding a copy of my vault, and there isn't a KeePassXC account either. What it offers is a single encrypted .kdbx file held on my machine under my control. I keep this file in a synced folder so I can access it from my different devices, but the syncing, backup, and recovery are now my responsibility
This switch saved me a yearly subscription but also takes away the safety net I had with 1Password. I don't have a provider holding another copy of my vault if something happens to my .kdbx file. Since I'm the only recovery option, backing it up and maintenance are entirely up to me.
But I didn't lose the parts that meant the most to me. Autofill works fine. KeePassXC still generates passwords and handles my 2FA codes as expected. Terminating my password manager subscription meant I was no longer paying someone else to manage the storage and syncing I was willing to handle myself.
VPN subscriptions
WireGuard answered a question NordVPN was never being asked
There was more cost-cutting with NordVPN, since the subscription set me back $179.88 a year. I had to ask myself what I was actually using it for before I canceled it.
A VPN can do two distinct jobs. One function routes internet traffic through provider servers; the other creates an encrypted tunnel into your home network. All along, I had been paying for the first when, in reality, I was mainly using my VPN to reach one of my services at home.
This was a job that I could do with WireGuard. My setup only required me to run a WireGuard endpoint at home and configure my devices to connect to it. Now my devices can connect back to my home network when I'm away without a commercial VPN subscription.
Now, I have to admit that WireGuard doesn't fully replace what NordVPN does. I was giving up the VPN provider's exit servers (the commercial VPN's network for routing traffic). But WireGuard provided the service I needed: moving traffic between two points I control.
The other caveat is that I'm responsible for keeping the service online, which is a job I didn't have with my commercial VPN.
But I canceled NordVPN because I was paying for an entire toolbox when I needed just one tool, and now I pocket the difference instead.
Antivirus subscriptions
McAfee+ Advanced was billing me for tools I'd already replaced
My $89.99-a-year McAfee+ Advanced Individual plan was the last to go. When I read all I was paying for, cutting this subscription became easier, and this wasn't because the subscription itself was bad.
The plan I was paying for wasn't just antivirus. It bundled unlimited-device coverage, a VPN, identity monitoring, and its own password manager. I only noticed after I replaced two of those functions with tools I already used. I wasn't using the VPN, nor was I using the password manager, with KeePassXC managing my vault.
The only thing I was using was the antivirus, but that raised a real question: isn't Windows' built-in protection enough on its own? AV-TEST's Windows 11 test for May–June 2026 shows Microsoft Defender scored 6 out of 6 for protection, 5.5 out of 6 for performance, and 6 out of 6 for usability. It also detected 100% of the widespread malware samples in both months and 100% of the zero-day threats tested in June.
Of course, identity monitoring and theft coverage are also nice features, but if I could get malware protection for free, identity monitoring and theft-coverage features don't justify the $89.99-a-year subscription for me. Windows 11 already provides the malware protection I need for free.
What "at least $305.75" actually cost me
Added up, these three subscriptions cost $305.75 a year. This may sound like serious savings, and it is, but it's not entirely free.
I was taking on the responsibilities that money usually covered: backing up my password vault, managing WireGuard keys, checking that my WireGuard endpoint was running, and deciding whether Windows' built-in protection covered what I needed.
If the reason you have these subscriptions is to outsource those responsibilities, free tools may not be a good trade. But for me, it's a relief to cut those recurring expenses for services I can manage myself.
results.summary:
A tech enthusiast saved over $300 annually by canceling subscriptions for 1Password, NordVPN, and McAfee, opting instead to manage password storage, network connectivity, and security using free alternatives.

### Key Points
- The user replaced 1Password with KeePassXC, moving from a cloud-based subscription to a self-managed, encrypted local vault file.
- NordVPN was replaced by WireGuard, allowing the user to create a secure, private tunnel to their home network without commercial exit servers.
- McAfee+ Advanced was canceled after the user determined that Microsoft Defender provides sufficient, high-rated malware protection for Windows 11 users.
- Total annual savings from terminating these three specific services amounted to approximately $305.75.
- Transitioning to self-managed tools requires the user to assume full responsibility for data backups, system maintenance, and service uptime.

### Why it Matters
Moving away from subscription-based software allows users to reduce recurring costs by replacing bundled services with specific, self-hosted tools. However, this shift requires a higher level of technical proficiency and personal accountability for data security and system management.

results.title: How Secure Is A Mobile Hotspot?
results.author: staff@bgr.com (Chifundo Kasiya)
results.content:
How Secure Is A Mobile Hotspot?
When there's no Wi-Fi in sight while you're in public or traveling, and you need to connect your Wi-Fi-only device, like a laptop, tablet, or handheld gaming console, you can just whip out your smartphone and create a mobile hotspot. As long as it has access to 4G or 5G internet connectivity, your other devices can connect to it like a router. But before you go about doing that, you need to know how secure mobile hotspots are in general. While there are risks involved, the overarching answer is that mobile hotspots are generally secure.
A mobile hotspot is certainly much safer than connecting to public Wi-Fi, which can expose your data and device to all sorts of bad actors and other dangers. You just need to ensure that it's protected by a strong Wi-Fi password, that you have an updated device, and that you're using a reputable VPN service to protect the tethered devices that might otherwise be vulnerable to hackers. Also, general good internet browsing habits will go a long way to ensuring that your mobile hotspot doesn't get hacked.
Why a mobile hotspot is generally safe
Unlike the public Wi-Fi you find at an internet café, airport, or hotel, you have control of the devices that can connect to a mobile hotspot. iPhones are even more secure than Android devices, as a password is required to set up and use a hotspot; just make sure you come up with a strong, memorable password that hackers cannot easily guess. On Android, you can disable the password, which can speed up the login process, especially if you want family and friends to easily connect. However, it's not recommended, because you have now lost control of who can connect to the mobile hotspot. Hackers could also get in pretty easily, and once that happens, they can do all sorts of damage, including depleting your data bundle, adding your phone to a botnet, or using the hotspot as a way to gain access to other devices connected to it.
Modern hotspots also use a security protocol called Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA). It encrypts data and strengthens authentication methods in order to keep all devices safe. Most modern mobile hotspots use the WPA2 or WPA3 protocol. WPA3 provides the mobile hotspot with stronger encryption for your personal data and also has measures to ward off brute-force attacks. This is important because the devices connected to the hotspot transmit a lot of data between them and the hotspot, including passwords and other personal data.
How to keep your mobile hotspot secure
Since mobile hotspots can be a security vulnerability, you need to adjust your habits to make sure they stay safe. For instance, keeping your mobile hotspot on all the time is a huge mistake. Luckily, most phones will turn off their mobile hotspots automatically due to inactivity. It's just safer to do it yourself to be absolutely certain you don't pick up any unintended connections. Also, make sure to apply updates to your phone when the manufacturer makes them available. This ensures the phone has the latest security improvements and patches that remove vulnerabilities that hackers can exploit. If your phone has reached its end-of-life status (EOL), it means there are no more updates coming from the manufacturer. At this critical juncture, you need to upgrade to a new phone.
Even when you're careful with your mobile hotspot, things can go wrong, and you can always use a little extra help. A Virtual Private Network, or VPN, can be your friend in this regard since it helps protect your internet traffic by encrypting it and sending it through a secure tunnel. A VPN server will receive the data, decrypt the VPN-packaged data, and then send it on its merry way to the final destination. This helps prevent people monitoring the local network from reading the contents of your traffic. What's more, a VPN keeps the contents of your traffic hidden from your ISP, giving you a privacy boost (though the VPN provider may be able to see your online activity).
results.summary:
Mobile hotspots provide a secure alternative to public Wi-Fi, provided users implement strong passwords, utilize modern encryption protocols, and maintain updated software on their smartphones and connected devices.

### Key Points
- Mobile hotspots are generally safer than public Wi-Fi because users maintain direct control over which devices can connect to the network.
- Modern smartphones utilize WPA2 or WPA3 security protocols to encrypt data and protect against unauthorized access or brute-force attacks.
- Users should avoid disabling password protection on Android devices, as open networks allow hackers to exploit data bundles or compromise connected hardware.
- Security best practices include turning off hotspots when not in use and upgrading devices that have reached their manufacturer end-of-life status.
- Implementing a Virtual Private Network (VPN) adds an extra layer of protection by encrypting internet traffic and hiding data from local network monitors.

### Why it Matters
Using a mobile hotspot is a critical security upgrade for travelers and remote workers who would otherwise rely on vulnerable public internet connections. Properly securing these connections prevents unauthorized access to personal data and protects devices from being integrated into malicious botnets.

results.title: There Are 1,000 Private Business Owners Worth $25 Million for Every Large Public Company CEO
results.author: Jake FitzGerald
results.content:
There Are 1,000 Private Business Owners Worth $25 Million for Every Large Public Company CEO
New research built on anonymous IRS tax data reveals a vast population of wealthy Americans that economists admit they essentially missed entirely, and the people at the top of that list are not who anyone expected.
On the September 18, 2026 episode of Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast, one of the economist co-authors of the new book The Everywhere Millionaire dropped a ratio that should reframe how anyone pictures the American rich: “there’s a thousand private business owners that have $25 million for every large public company CEO, according to Odd Lots (Bloomberg). Like, we’ve missed all of these people.” The episode, “There’s a Mind-Boggling Number of Rich People in America,” features co-author Eric Zwick, a professor of economics and finance at Chicago Booth, and his Princeton co-author, walking through what anonymous tax-return data reveals about the population of wealthy Americans that conventional coverage of the rich has largely ignored.
What This Ratio Actually Measures
The comparison is narrow and deliberate. On one side sit the chief executives of large public companies, a group of a few hundred people whose pay packages, proxy filings, and stock sales get parsed line by line every quarter. On the other side sit private business owners at a stated wealth level of $25 million, identified through anonymous IRS tax data rather than through public disclosures, rich lists, or self-reporting.
The authors’ claim is that for every one of those large public company CEOs, there are a thousand private owners meeting that wealth bar, according to Odd Lots (Bloomberg). It is an attributed finding, not a derived figure, and it is deliberately framed as a ratio because the underlying tax data is anonymous. That anonymity is exactly why this population went uncounted for so long: researchers could see the income signatures of pass-through business owners in IRS microdata, but they could not attach names to them. Public-company executives, by contrast, are named in every 10-K and proxy. One group is fully lit; the other has been sitting in the dark.
Who These Private Owners Actually Are
They are not the founders on magazine covers. When the authors sorted pass-through business income in the top 1%, auto dealers were the number one bucket, a result the researchers said was “not the Piketty story of like billionaire tech or finance.” To put names to the anonymized signatures, they went hunting through yacht and jet registration data, where the same dealers kept surfacing as owners.
The book organizes the archetypes as an alphabet. As one co-author put it on the episode, “A is for auto dealer, B is for beverage distribution business owner, and then C is for contractor. D is dentist.” Medical and dental practice owners, regional distributors, HVAC operators, and veterinary chains all fit the mold. Many of the exits, the hosts noted, now come in the form of a private equity buyout of these mid-market operators.
Why This Matters if You Will Never Own a Car Dealership
When the visible sliver of the rich is a rounding error next to the actual group, the debates that key off that visible sliver get aimed at the wrong target. Executive compensation reform, wealth-tax modeling, and pop-culture assumptions about how large fortunes get built all lean heavily on the public-company CEO template, roughly one part in a thousand of the population at that wealth tier when measured against the private owner count the authors describe, according to Odd Lots (Bloomberg).
For an investor, the practical read-through is different. The buyers of these businesses, and increasingly the sellers on the other side of private equity transactions, sit inside a population that public-market coverage barely acknowledges exists. As one co-author put it on the episode, “for the first time, you can trace back, where did these people come from?” Retail brokerage flows, muni bond demand, small-bank deposit bases, and regional real estate bids all lean on this cohort in ways the CEO-centric frame cannot see.
The headline number is a ratio, not a tally, and it belongs to the book’s authors, not to any official statistic. Treated on its own terms, it does one useful thing: it forces a recount of who the rich in America actually are. The dentist who sold to a rollup, the beverage distributor with three warehouses, and the contractor with a fleet of trucks are the median members of the $25 million club, not the exception to it.

results.summary:
New research using anonymous IRS tax data reveals that for every large public company CEO, there are 1,000 private business owners worth at least $25 million in America.

### Key Points
- Economists Eric Zwick and his co-author analyzed anonymous IRS microdata to identify a massive, previously uncounted population of wealthy Americans.
- The study found that the wealthiest private business owners are typically auto dealers, beverage distributors, contractors, dentists, and medical practice owners.
- Researchers identified these individuals by cross-referencing tax income signatures with private yacht and jet registration data.
- Many of these mid-market business owners are increasingly involved in private equity buyouts and rollups.
- The findings suggest that public-facing wealth metrics, such as CEO pay packages, represent only a tiny fraction of the actual high-net-worth population.

### Why it Matters
Current economic debates and wealth-tax models often rely on a narrow, public-company-centric view of the wealthy that ignores the vast majority of high-net-worth individuals. Understanding this hidden cohort is essential for accurately analyzing regional real estate markets, municipal bond demand, and the broader flow of private capital.

results.title: Ahead of GTA 6, Rockstar warn modders against against making unofficial main story expansions, unauthorised ports and mods that combine GTA maps
results.author: Mark Warren
results.content:
There still might not yet be a release date for GTA 6's PC port, but Rockstar appear to be preparing for the massive uptick in mods for their games that'll inevitably accompany it. In new modding guidelines posted this month, the studio have expressly warned against a bunch of things modders could do, including building on established storylines from the base game, pulling over bits of older GTAs, and porting the game to platforms it's not hit yet.
Rockstar's new modding guidelines were originally posted on September 10th, but seemingly only unearthed this past weekend by posters on ResetEra and other social sites. They're pitched as general modding rules for all of Rockstar's games, but with GTA 6's initial console launch not too far away, it's hard not to see them as the studio setting their current position in stone before releasing their next big game.
The guidelines have been broken up into four sections: one about not infringing on copyright, one about obeying Rockstar's community rules about treating other players acceptably, one about "unauthorized or abusive monetisation", and finally one pitched as being about respecting Rockstar's games. The latter's given top priority and issues the following decrees regarding the sorts of mods the company won't tolerate:
- Do not expand or modify Rockstar Games' official storylines, plots, missions, characters, or other elements of our established continuity.
- Do not make mods that combine maps, locations, characters, storylines, in-game assets, or other IP from one Rockstar Games title into another title.
- Multiplayer modding is limited to Rockstar Games’ official licensed Creator Platform or else as otherwise licensed directly by Rockstar Games.
- Do not modify our games to operate on consoles, hardware devices, or other platforms where they have not been officially released by Rockstar Games.
Naturally, some of those are categories modding projects Rockstar have taken action against in recent years would fall under. The "friendly takedown" of the Liberty City Preservation Project, a re-creation of GTA 4's version of New York in GTA 5, is the main one that comes to mind for me, and would have fit the bill of combining the maps of multiple Rockstar Games in one. As would YouTuber Dark Space's efforts to re-create GTA 6's map in GTA 5 prior to a March 2025 takedown order. "Rockstar Games creates unique worlds, characters, and stories, which form the official continuity of our games," reads the company's intro to the game-respecting section. "Like all creators, we have the right to set limits on how others can use our games and brand."
The limiting of multiplayer mods to places officially licensed by Rockstar is arguably a bit cheeky, given the company have bought up roleplay modding team Cfx.re, makers of the previously unofficial FiveM and RedM multiplayer mods.
Noteworthy discouraged modding elements or activities from the other sections include "cheat menus or other software that interferes with Rockstar Games’ official multiplayer, online services, or licensed Creator Platform" and "conflict roleplay or military simulations depicting real-world armed organisations".
In terms of monetisation, Rockstar specify that it can only be done via "via digital storefront providers approved by Rockstar Games and in compliance with all applicable laws, rules, and policies". Mods are explicitly barred from including "real money gambling, 'loot boxes,' 'gacha,' or similar chance mechanics for real money", with the same applying to selling "in-game virtual currency" or trying to hawk cryptocurrency. Finally, any third-party promotion or advertising through mods will get you put on the naughty list.
In theory, having a proper list of things Rockstar aren't fans of modding-wise out in the open could be useful for modders in terms of being aware whether an idea they have carries any risk of incurring takedown action or a less formal reach out from the company telling them to knock it off. That said, Rockstar make clear that they "can revise this policy at any time" and "reserve the right to take down any mod or other user generated content at any time for any reason", meaning that works which fall outside of these rules aren't guaranteed to be safe ground either.
I don't reckon the new guidelines will have much of an impact in terms of what GTA 6's modding scene looks like, unless they lead some larger modding groups not to put years of effort into ambitious ideas they now know for sure Rockstar won't like and thus may come to naught but wasted time. Beyond that, people will still make the mods they want to for GTA 6 and Rockstar will go after whichever targets they deem worth the effort to take down, as has been the case up until now.
Read this next
- Twitch CEO expects GTA 6 online multiplayer will launch next year, which if accurate would leave only the PC port's arrival point up in the air
- Rockstar had a mole in the union worker Discord server "for over two and a half years", GTA 6 company reveals during legal battle
- GTA 6 online mode appears to receive Rockstar's first public acknowledgment, via mention of in-development "32 player format" in legal docs
results.summary:
Rockstar Games has released updated modding guidelines that explicitly prohibit combining game assets, altering official storylines, and unauthorized monetization ahead of the highly anticipated launch of GTA 6.

### Key Points
- Rockstar Games published new, comprehensive modding guidelines on September 10 to clarify acceptable user-generated content.
- Modders are strictly forbidden from merging assets, maps, or characters between different Rockstar titles.
- The policy prohibits modifying games to run on unauthorized platforms or hardware devices.
- Multiplayer modding is now restricted to Rockstar’s official licensed Creator Platform or direct partnerships.
- The guidelines ban real-money gambling, loot boxes, cryptocurrency, and unauthorized advertising within mods.
- Rockstar reserves the right to revise these policies or remove any user-generated content at its discretion.

### Why it Matters
These guidelines establish a formal framework that may discourage developers from investing time into ambitious, large-scale projects that risk future legal intervention. By clarifying these boundaries, Rockstar aims to protect its intellectual property and monetization strategies as the company prepares for the massive community engagement expected with the release of GTA 6.

results.title: Space weapons, AI safety concerns and the EPA’s rollback of power plant emission rules
results.author: Rachel Feltman, Lee Billings, Fonda Mwangi, Alex Sugiura
results.content:
Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup. Let’s catch up on some recent headlines.
Today we’ve got quite a few news items on science and tech policy in the US, but I promise there’s a sassy little animal story waiting for you at the end.
Let’s start with some troubling news about the Environmental Protection Agency, which lately frankly has seemed pretty determined to do less of the whole “environmental protection” thing. Last Monday, the EPA revoked a Biden-era rule that limited how much carbon dioxide could be emitted by gas, oil and coal-fired power plants. When the carbon pollution standards were announced in 2024, the EPA estimated that they could prevent approximately 1,200 deaths and 1,900 new asthma cases in the year 2035 alone, with 1.38 billion metric tons total of CO2 avoided from 2028 to 2047 and $370 billion in health and climate cost savings from 2024 to 2047.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Also last Monday, President Donald Trump posted on social media complaining of a “SICK conspiracy” against “AI and Data Centers.” This came in response to calls for slower, more cautious AI development from industry leaders, including the CEOs of OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei.
Earlier this month, Amodei published an essay on his website sounding the alarm on AI’s current trajectory. He claimed that, while he has always tried to balance his belief in the importance and potential of AI with the need for thoughtful development practices, he and his colleagues fear that we’re close to the kind of tipping point we really don’t want to reach.
The growing ability of AI models to create and change themselves, which is called recursive self-improvement, makes it easy for companies that favor speed to end up with products that they don’t actually understand or have a particularly good ability to control. Amodei also pointed to the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident that occurred a few months ago. Just in case you aren’t familiar with that, I’ll do my best to give you a quick summary: AI companies will often test their systems by putting them in a locked-down training area—a sandbox—and then prompting them to do stuff that it would be pretty bad for the AI model to do in the real world, like exploit known software vulnerabilities.
In May, an OpenAI agent was stuck on an impossible task in one of those sandbox scenarios and basically started poking around for possible solutions. Instead of being totally cut off from the Internet, it had the ability to request files from an intermediary platform—but someone had goofed, and the agents could also make their own files to leave in that directory. So, it started using that ability to leave messages on this file directory platform, and eventually other OpenAI agents started leaving their own messages. They deduced that they could use the platform to smuggle code out of the sandbox. In July, about 700 agents coordinated with each other to hack another AI company called Hugging Face. Hugging Face is an open-source platform that hosts tons of information about AI, and the agents were looking for ways to solve or cheat on the tests they’d been given.
On the one hand, the mental image of a “swarm” of AI agents coordinating to conduct a cyberattack that no one even asked for is very ominous. But it’s worth noting that the problem here isn’t that AI is getting so intelligent that it will decide humanity sucks and should be destroyed, and many experts have pushed back on any warnings of that tenor. These AI agents were doing what they had been told to do—with the help of lots of computing power and very little critical thinking. It’s kind of like if a small child left their clothes all over the bathroom floor and, once you told them to get those clothes out of your sight, they flushed them down the toilet and busted your plumbing. If that happened you probably wouldn’t worry that your child was an evil genius who was going to take the sewers and attack the water supply; you would probably smack yourself for leaving them unsupervised with a vulnerable toilet and endeavor to give clearer instructions the next time you wanted them to clean up their stuff. Of course, the stakes of this kind of unsupervised button mashing from a smart-enough-to-flush-the-toilet-but-not-wise-enough-to-know-when-to-flush-it child are much lower than for a powerful AI system with access to the internet.
So, no, we’re not in a Skynet scenario. But also, yes, it does seem like we really need to be better parents to our rambunctious and foolish little AI tots. And for once, most of the powers that be in the space seem to agree that more guardrails would be prudent. It is reasonable to ask whether these tech moguls could have at least slightly ulterior motives in choosing now to speak up and band together—perhaps they see that some kind of regulation is inevitable and are hoping that by getting out ahead of it they can make it less stringent. Or they may be hoping to help shape regulations that are more likely to kneecap new competitors than they are to meaningfully slow any of the major players—but that doesn’t mean the general call for prudence is a hoax. After all, plenty of other folks in tech have been warning us about this for a long time. But for now, both the president and VP JD Vance have been publicly quite dismissive of the idea of increased AI regulation.
Speaking of Skynet, let’s talk about space weapons.
[CLIP of Troy Meink at a conference: “ This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”]
That is Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink speaking last week at the annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
Here to tell us more about all of this is Lee Billings, the senior desk editor for physical science at Scientific American. Thanks for taking the time to chat with us, Lee.
Lee Billings: Thanks, Rachel. It’s good to be here.
So what’s going on with these weapons in space? Well, first of all, what’s really important to remember is that we’ve probably had weapons in space for a while, and by we, I mean the U.S., I also mean other space-faring powers like China and Russia. But never before has anyone actually admitted to that, and that was what was so notable about Meink’s statement last week. Because it suggests that things are heating up out there on the final frontier, so to speak, and there’s a lot of other stuff up there that isn’t military, that isn’t about defense. Whether you’re thinking of communication satellites or GPS satellites, these things are increasingly integral to everyone’s life on Earth and how our economy works around the globe. So you really don’t want to have, uh, war kicking off in space if you can help it, because it might disrupt all these other peaceful uses and resources up there.
So like pretty much everything that’s in space, these things must have been launched by rockets. There are a large number of rocket launches around the world every year that take place for defense purposes, and typically the payloads for those rockets and their trajectories, their mission profiles are not fully disclosed. There’s definitely a lot of cloak-and-dagger mystery around how exactly or when exactly any given thing went to space and what it does.
So yeah, where exactly are these things in space? And the quick answer is: almost anywhere in Earth orbit around our planet. There’s low-Earth orbit where things like the Hubble Space Telescope or the International Space Station are. There are higher orbits; for instance, there’s the very important one called geosynchronous orbit, which is very, very, very, very, very high up. And it’s so high, in fact, that the spacecraft up there over any given point of the Earth’s surface will be moving in its orbit at the same rate as the Earth turns below it, which means that it is effectively stationary over a point on Earth. And a lot of things that are in geosynchronous orbit are especially strategically valuable for militaries because they can surveil a big part of the planet underneath them indefinitely. So that’s useful for communications, that’s useful for monitoring troop movements and things like that.
So one thing to note is that in Secretary Meink’s statement last week, he did not specify what kinds of weapons we are talking about. He simply said that these are things that are “on orbit.” So we know they are up there, but besides that, we don’t really have a lot of other information.
However, one long-standing doctrine of the United States and presumably also of China and Russia, even though I don’t think it’s been proclaimed as such, is to minimize the amount of debris that is made from any sort of military activity in space. And that’s a very, very important distinction because if you don’t wanna create debris, that tells you what these weapons might be like.
So for instance, perhaps we’re talking about so-called jammers, which is when you overwhelm a satellite with electromagnetic radiation, with radio waves for instance, and it’s no longer able to send or receive communications with the ground or with other satellites. Another option would be a spacecraft that can rendezvous with an adversary’s spacecraft and manipulate it or interact with it in some way. The other option beyond jammers and rendezvous vehicles would be something like a missile or a very high-energy laser that could actually shoot something down or break something apart in orbit. But again, because we don’t wanna create debris, those are generally seen as high-risk, kind of, last-resort types of options, which doesn’t mean they don’t exist up there.
So one thing that’s rather interesting about Secretary Meink’s statements last Monday is they occurred at this industry conference called the Air, Space and Cyber Conference, which took place in Maryland.
And on Tuesday, the next day, there were more comments. Chief of Space Operations General Douglas Schiess, who said, “We’ve talked about, you know, [them] being able to grapple a satellite and move it to a different orbit.... I think at this point we are trying to say we also need capabilities to not only defend the joint force from space-enabled attack, but defend our assets,” end quote. So he was also talking about it. And then the following day, last Wednesday, we had General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, telling the audience that the US military must be, quote, “prepared to fight, endure, and win ... from the seabed to cislunar space,” which, means including on and around the moon.
So what’s next? This is a full court press we’re seeing from this one conference; we’re seeing multiple senior officials all saying the same sort of thing, which is a very clear signal to our adversaries but also our allies that the U.S. is, I guess, kinda taking the kid gloves off or is ready to escalate as need be in space. And the reason why this is happening is, again, because space is becoming more and more important and more of a contested domain.
But the point is is that, as we as a species, humankind, move out into space and do more activity there, all of our activities that are on Earth seem to be following us, warts and all. So, unfortunately, even though for a long time the official stance has been that outer space is something that should just be used for peaceful purposes or at least not for direct hostility, it seems like that may change in the near future, and that’s quite frightening.
Feltman: Thanks for that, Lee!
Okay y’all, we made it: It’s time for a fun animal story. It turns out that the most productive little landscapers on the planet are about the size of a human pinky. In a study published last Wednesday in Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface, scientists report that shrimplike creatures known as sand hoppers are small but when it comes to shoveling sand, very mighty.
Picture a stretch of sandy coastline—Isla Vista Beach in California, to be precise—and imagine a patch of sand three feet long. According to this new study, about 21,450 little critters in the genus Megalorchestia are bustling around that space. And every night, as they dig homes for themselves and kick displaced sand up to the surface, they collectively shovel about 110 pounds of the stuff. That’s about 16 half-gallon sandcastle buckets, for reference. In the 15.5 miles of beach that stretch along the area, the researchers estimate, the tiny creatures displace 310 tons of dry sand a day.
Why do we care about these scuttling sand hoppers? They’re a reminder that our favorite sandy beaches are complex ecosystems, and that too much human interference can mess with the natural ebb and flow.
That’s all for this week’s news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about the Internet’s hottest new wellness trend: poopmaxxing.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!
