results.title: Cyber insurance gap leaves UK property businesses dangerously exposed: GlobalData
results.author: Douglas Blakey
results.content:
Cyber insurance remains underpenetrated among the UK real estate and renting businesses, despite cyberattacks against UK property services companies increasing by 17% in 2025. A combination of rising cyber exposure and relatively low insurance uptake is leaving a significant proportion of property businesses financially exposed to cyber incidents, reveals GlobalData, publishers of Life Insurance International.
GlobalData Q1 2025 UK SME Insurance Survey
GlobalData’s Q1 2025 UK SME Insurance Survey found that cyber insurance penetration in the real estate and renting industry is below the total SME market across every business size. Penetration stands at 7.7% among sole traders, 15.8% among micro businesses, 20.5% among small businesses, and 55.0% among medium-sized businesses. This compares with 13.1%, 26.4%, 40.1%, and 63.0%, respectively, across the wider SME market.
Access deeper industry intelligence
Experience unmatched clarity with a single platform that combines unique data, AI, and human expertise.
The findings come as cyber threats facing property businesses continue to increase. Figures sourced from the Information Commissioner’s Office show that cyberattacks against UK property services businesses rose from 178 incidents in 2024 to 208 in 2025. Property companies routinely handle sensitive customer information, including bank details, mortgage information, tenancy records, proof of address, passports, and driving licenses, increasing both the value of their data to cybercriminals and the potential consequences of a breach.
The financial risks extend beyond the loss of personal information. Criminals can use compromised property transaction data to redirect payments by replacing legitimate bank details during transactions. City of London Police and Action Fraud recorded 143 cases of conveyancing fraud between April 2024 and March 2025, resulting in losses of £11.7m ($15.6m). Most cases involved residential property transactions, with an average loss of £78,393.
Charlie Hutcherson, Senior Insurance Analyst at GlobalData, comments: “Property businesses are becoming increasingly reliant on digital systems while continuing to hold large amounts of sensitive personal and financial information.”
Market opportunity for insurers
This creates a broad cyber risk that stretches beyond data breaches to include fraud, business interruption, and potentially significant recovery costs. However, cyber insurance uptake across the sector has not kept pace with this exposure, particularly among smaller businesses.
Hutcherson continues: “For insurers, this represents an opportunity to address an increasingly visible protection gap. Improving understanding of cyber risks among property businesses will be important, but insurers will also need to make cover easier to understand and access.”
Smaller firms may not necessarily recognise the full financial impact a cyber incident can have until one occurs, meaning brokers and insurers have an important role to play in demonstrating how insurance can sit alongside cybersecurity measures.
Hutcherson concludes: “As property transactions and customer interactions become increasingly digital, cyber exposure within the sector is unlikely to diminish. Rising attack volumes combined with comparatively low insurance penetration could increase the number of businesses absorbing cyber losses themselves. Insurers that can improve awareness, simplify distribution, and demonstrate the practical value of cyber cover therefore have an opportunity to increase penetration within an underserved part of the SME market.”
results.summary:
UK property and real estate businesses face growing cyber threats, yet insurance adoption remains significantly lower than the broader SME market, leaving many firms financially vulnerable to attacks.

### Key Points
- Cyberattacks against UK property services companies rose by 17% in 2025, reaching 208 reported incidents.
- Cyber insurance penetration in the real estate sector lags behind the wider SME market across all business sizes.
- Conveyancing fraud resulted in £11.7 million in losses between April 2024 and March 2025, with 143 recorded cases.
- Property firms are high-value targets due to the sensitive financial and personal data they store for transactions.
- Medium-sized property businesses report a 55% insurance uptake, while sole traders remain the least protected at 7.7%.

### Why it Matters
- The widening protection gap leaves many property firms exposed to significant financial losses from data breaches and payment redirection fraud. Insurers have a clear opportunity to capture this underserved market by simplifying coverage and better educating small business owners on digital risks.

results.title: Google hit with €403m fine by Irish data watchdog over GDPR violations
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
results.content:
- Published
Google has been fined €403m (£345m) by the Republic of Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) over its handling of location data.
The penalty - one of the largest of its kind imposed by the Irish watchdog authority - followed an inquiry launched into the tech giant six years ago, following complaints from several European consumer rights organisations.
On Monday the DPC said its investigation found Google had processed data in a manner that was not "lawful", "fair" or "transparent".
The inquiry concerned Google's processing of location data in three specific features - Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy between 25 May 2018 to 4 February 2020.
Location data is any kind of data which can be used to infer a person's location.
It can "reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private", said DPC deputy commissioner Graham Doyle in a statement released on Monday.
The report said Google's practices "infringed" General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) - legislation that came into effect on 25 May, 2018, creating strict data privacy and security law within the European Union (EU).
Doyle added: "The GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA (European Economic Area), and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner."
He continued: "As a result of Google's failures... individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data.
"The retention of users' location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control."
In addition to being fined, Google has also been ordered to bring its data processing into compliance within six months.
How have Google responded?
In a statement, Google said: "This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we've significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple."
They also said they have made data protection improvements in recent years, including "industry-first auto-delete controls", which enables all users to "set your account to automatically delete your data on a rolling three, 18, or 36-month basis".
Other measures to safeguard personal data have also been introduced, they said, such as "simple ads management", which allows you "to turn off personalized ads entirely", and "increased transparency", including "consolidated detailed information about our location data practices and account settings".
results.summary:
The Irish Data Protection Commission has fined Google €403 million for failing to process user location data in a lawful, fair, and transparent manner under GDPR regulations.

### Key Points
- The Irish Data Protection Commission issued the €403 million penalty following a six-year investigation into Google's data practices.
- The inquiry focused on the processing of location data within Web & App Activity, Location History, and Location Accuracy features.
- Regulators found that Google infringed on GDPR requirements between May 2018 and February 2020 by failing to provide sufficient transparency.
- Google must bring its data processing operations into full compliance with EU privacy laws within the next six months.
- Google stated the findings concern historical policies and noted that it has since introduced auto-delete controls and improved transparency tools.

### Why it Matters
This ruling highlights the ongoing regulatory pressure on major tech companies to maintain strict compliance with European data privacy standards. It reinforces the importance of user consent and data minimization, potentially forcing further changes to how global platforms manage and retain sensitive personal information.

results.title: I ran Autoruns on my Windows PC and discovered startup services I'd completely forgotten about
results.author: Simon Batt
results.content:
If you want to check everything that runs on startup when you're on a Windows PC, which tool do you reach for first? There's a good chance you open up Task Manager and check the Startup tab, which, while useful, doesn't give you the whole picture. As such, if you want to do a deep dive on what your PC is doing, you're going to want to use Autoruns.
Autoruns is a deep dive into your Windows 11 PC
It finds things that your default apps won't find
Autoruns is a free app you can grab off the Microsoft Ignite Sysinternals website. If you want, you can run it off Sysinternals Live, but if you want something you can throw on a USB stick and use on all of your computers, you can download the executables, too. For the sake of this article, I downloaded the executables.
Here's how the developer describes Autorun:
                        Simply run Autoruns and it shows you the currently configured auto-start applications as well as the full list of Registry and file system locations available for auto-start configuration. Autostart locations displayed by Autoruns include logon entries, Explorer add-ons, Internet Explorer add-ons including Browser Helper Objects (BHOs), Appinit DLLs, image hijacks, boot execute images, Winlogon notification DLLs, Windows Services and Winsock Layered Service Providers, media codecs, and more.
Sounds great on paper, but how does it perform in reality? Fortunately, it does everything you want, and more. In fact, it completely blows Task Manager out of the water, which I'll cover later in the article.
Getting Autoruns to sniff out your processes is really simple
You just need to get it set up properly
For this article, I've sicced Autoruns on my Windows 11 Shadow PC. I use this cloud PC exclusively for gaming, so it may not have as much detritus on it as a daily driver; however, it has been marinading for about two or three years, so it has had plenty of time to accumulate digital gunk in its folders.
To get Autoruns working, I grabbed the executables from the download page, right-clicked the Autoruns64 executable, and selected Run as Administrator. It's important to give it elevated access; it may not have the permissions to get deep into your system files otherwise. Once you have it running, accept the disclaimer.
Now, you need to ask yourself: how much do you trust yourself not to accidentally shut off an important Windows service? Regardless of your answer, click on Options at the top. You'll see four entries:
- Hide Empty Locations
- Hide Microsoft Entries
- Hide Windows Entries
- Hide VirusTotal Clean Entries
If you're like me and you're worried that you'll hit a load-bearing service that will send your PC crashing down, ensure that both Microsoft and Windows entries are hidden. That way, it won't show you anything vital to your system. Likewise, if you're feeling brave, ask it to show everything and see what your system is doing.
Now that you're up and running, take a look at the list. Anything highlighted in yellow is missing its core files, and anything in pink means it doesn't have a verified digital signature. That doesn't mean everything in pink is definitely malware, but it's still worth giving them a second look just in case. My results were pretty good, but I did find a service I don't remember ever installing, and two video game anti-cheat systems that had lingered even long after I had uninstalled them!
If you want to stop a service from running, but you're concerned about deleting it outright, you can disable it instead. To do that, uncheck the box to the left of the service name. That'll free up your resources, and if anything goes horrifically wrong, you can just check it again.
Autoruns does a far better job than Task Manager
It's not even close
So, why don't people just use the Task Manager to find startup processes? Well, you can see my results in the screenshot above. Exact same PC, exact same time as when I ran Autoruns, but far fewer services listed. This is because Task Manager doesn't look everywhere that Autoruns does, plus it gives you far more permissions that Microsoft hides from users to prevent them from damaging their system.
As such, Autoruns is a lot riskier, and if you're not sure what you're doing, you can do far worse damage to your system stability than Task Manager. However, if you move carefully, research each process, and disable services instead of nuking them outright, you should be fine.
Autoruns does what Windows doesn't
If you truly want to dig into your system and see what's still ticking over, Autoruns does the job. With great power comes great responsibility, but as long as you're careful (and you disable system-important services from your view), you should be fine.
results.summary:
The Microsoft Sysinternals tool Autoruns provides a comprehensive, deep-level view of Windows startup processes and registry configurations that far exceeds the capabilities of the standard Windows Task Manager.

### Key Points
- Autoruns is a free utility available via the Microsoft Sysinternals website or Sysinternals Live.
- The software identifies auto-start locations including Explorer add-ons, Windows Services, media codecs, and boot execute images.
- Users can filter results by hiding Microsoft and Windows entries to prevent accidental system instability.
- Color-coded alerts highlight missing files in yellow and unverified digital signatures in pink.
- The tool allows users to disable services by unchecking boxes, providing a safer alternative to permanent deletion.

### Why it Matters
This utility offers advanced users and IT professionals granular control over system resources and hidden background processes. By exposing deep-level startup items, it helps identify lingering software, potential malware, and unnecessary services that standard Windows tools often overlook.

results.title: Hash Identifier Tools – Command-Line Password Hash Identification
results.author: Darknet
results.content:
I tested hashID 3.1.4 and Name-That-Hash 1.11.0 against the same hash samples. Both recognised $2a$ bcrypt but rejected the otherwise identical $2b$ sample. Only Name-That-Hash recognised the Argon2id sample.
Both tools were installed through pip and tested on 6 September 2026.
Two others worth knowing, haiti and hashcat, are at the end as alternatives. I didn’t run those, and I say so where they appear.
Different formats, the same hexadecimal shape
Start with the MD5 of the word password, a bare 32-character hexadecimal string. Ask hashID what it is, and it returns eighteen possibilities; ask Name-That-Hash and it returns twenty-four. Both are right to.
MD5, NTLM, LM, MD4, the Domain Cached Credentials formats and a dozen others all produce exactly 128 bits of hex, and nothing in the string itself separates them.
Take a concrete case. The empty LM hash constant aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee – the value that fills the LM field of a Windows credential dump whenever the LM hash is blank – produces the same shapeless list from both tools, headed by MD5 and NTLM.
Both tools returned candidate lists for this sample rather than identifying it specifically as the empty LM constant. For the common hexadecimal formats, an identifier narrows the field and then hands the real decision back to you.
Provenance – which system produced the hash, which file it sat in – resolves what the string cannot. So the identifiers earn their keep on formats that carry a self-describing prefix, and that’s where they start to differ.
The 2026 blind spot both common tools share
bcrypt hashes announce themselves with a version prefix. Give both tools a classic $2a$ bcrypt hash, and both identify it correctly – hashID offers bcrypt alongside its two aliases, Name-That-Hash the same. Now change the a to a b in the prefix, making it $2b$ and leaving everything else identical:
| 1 2 3 4 5 | $ hashid '$2b$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy' [+] Unknown hash $ nth -t '$2b$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy' No hashes found. | 
Both fail. $2b$ isn’t an exotic variant. Python’s maintained bcrypt library generates $2b$ by default, so passwords hashed through that path today land in this form unless the caller overrides the prefix.
Two different identifiers, both a single pip command away, and neither recognises a current bcrypt prefix while both handle the older $2a$.
The reported bcrypt results use a 60-character sample; the earlier malformed sample was excluded.
Where the two identifiers diverge
They part company on Argon2, the algorithm that won the Password Hashing Competition and that current guidance names first for new password storage. Given an Argon2id string, hashID returns Unknown hash; Name-That-Hash returns Argon2id. That’s the clearest difference in capability between them.
hashID’s pattern table hasn’t changed since 2015. In this test, it missed both $2b$ and Argon2id; Name-That-Hash recognised Argon2id but shared the $2b$ miss.
The $2b$ prefix dates from 2014, before hashID’s March 2015 release, so it’s a gap the tool never covered, not one that opened up under it. Argon2id does post-date it, and the frozen table is the obvious explanation for that miss.
On the MD5 sample, Name-That-Hash also returned the longer list, twenty-four against hashID’s eighteen, though that’s one input and not a census of either tool’s rules. Of the two, it’s the better-informed on this set. But more maintained isn’t the same as complete: the $2b$ gap belongs to both.
Other maintained options, not tested here
Two more tools are worth knowing, and both were outside what I could run here – the environment had neither a Ruby runtime nor a hashcat build. So what follows is drawn from their documentation and source, not from a test. Read it as a pointer, not a result standing alongside the two above.
haiti is a Ruby identifier that’s actively developed, with a v4 release in early 2026 and recent commits. Its documented draw is that it returns the matching hashcat and John the Ripper references beside each candidate, which is the detail you want if identification is a step toward cracking.
It installs as a gem rather than through pip. Whether it clears the $2b$ bar that both tested tools failed is exactly the claim I won’t make without running it.
And if the next step is a crack, identification may not need a separate tool at all. hashcat carries an --identify option, documented in its own usage text as showing all supported algorithms for an input hash.
Asking hashcat directly removes a translation step between an identifier’s naming and hashcat’s mode numbers. That option is in hashcat’s source; I didn’t run it here.
What to actually use
When Darknet covered hashID in 2017, the page already noted it hadn’t been updated since 2015. This comparison asks whether moving to a maintained identifier closes that gap. For $2b$, it doesn’t.
For a quick look at a hash you already have context for, either pip-installable identifier is fine, and Name-That-Hash is the better-informed of the two: it knows more recent formats, and it’s still maintained. Keep hashID’s limits in mind – this site’s closer look at hashID lays out the full extent of its 2015 freeze.
If you’re working toward a crack, let hashcat identify the hash it’s about to attack. And if identification is a recurring part of your workflow, haiti’s cracker-reference output is worth the gem install.
Tested 6 September 2026. hashID v3.1.4 and Name-That-Hash 1.11.0 were run against a fixed hash set; haiti and hashcat were not run in this environment, and their behaviour is cited from documentation and source, as noted above.
results.summary:
A comparative analysis of hash identification tools hashID 3.1.4 and Name-That-Hash 1.11.0 reveals significant gaps in recognizing modern password hashing formats like the $2b$ bcrypt prefix.

### Key Points
- Both hashID and Name-That-Hash failed to identify the $2b$ bcrypt hash format during testing on 6 September 2026.
- Name-That-Hash successfully identified Argon2id, whereas hashID returned an "Unknown hash" result for the same input.
- Both tools struggled to uniquely identify common hexadecimal formats like MD5, often returning broad lists of potential candidates.
- hashID has not received significant pattern table updates since 2015, limiting its effectiveness with newer cryptographic standards.
- Alternative tools like haiti and hashcat offer deeper integration with cracking software, providing direct references for security professionals.

### Why it Matters
Reliable hash identification is critical for security researchers and administrators who must determine the correct algorithm before attempting password recovery or auditing. Relying on outdated tools can lead to misidentification or failure to recognize modern, secure hashing standards, necessitating the use of actively maintained alternatives.

results.title: The Comedians You Should and Will Know of 2026
results.author: X González, X González, X González
results.content:
It’s tougher than ever to track who’s going to make it in the comedy industry and how they’ll get there. SNL is still functioning after 50 years, and there’s a shiny, new version across the pond. But the White House Correspondents’ Dinner has devolved significantly since its glory days atop the comedy calendar, proving to be a weaker platform for political satire than the Onion’s takeover of Infowars. One of the last historic network late-night shows was recently forced into retirement, while Netflix and YouTube are leaning deeper into cheaper and shanefully less ambitious spins on the format called “video podcasts.” A former POTUS executive produced an HBO sketch series starring Larry David in silly wigs that sparked zero buzz; contrast that with independent creator Druski, who continues to build a sprawling digital sketch-comedy empire with millions of fans outside the traditional system.
The career paths couldn’t be more divergent for the comedians featured on our 12th annual list of Comedians You Should and Will Know. Here you’ll find Dropouts, TikTokers, road dogs, competition winners, shitposters, Brits, and clowns. They’re on tour, in clubs, online, and in writers’ rooms. After polling over 200 comedy-scene experts — including sources at comedy clubs, festivals, late-night shows, improv theaters, TV networks, podcast studios, record labels, production companies, and film studios, as well as comedians previously featured on this list — we came away with dozens of comedians at the top of their game. From there, we watched a lot of Reels, specials, live sets, and podcast appearances and got into many long philosophical debates to choose the 19 comedians producing the most distinctive work right now.
Meet the Comedians:
Jack Bensinger | Dukes | Grace Johnson | Hayden Johnson | Li Jin Hao | Ania Magliano | Janet McNamara | Courtney O’Donnell | Milan Patel | Hassan Phills | Taneshia “Just Nesh” Rice | Ethan Simmons-Patterson | Ron Taylor | Sureni Weerasekera | Lou Wilson | Ivy Wolk | Xhloe and Natasha
Jack Bensinger
Jack Bensinger’s comedic universe is Saw-esque, filled with traps ensuring no character he creates will ever see things go their way. He delights in the freaky, the grotesque, and especially the embarrassing. Look no further than “The Nudemans,” a 2026 sketch the comedian wrote during his first year working as a writer on SNL, in which a flummoxed Andrew Dismukes can’t figure out how to behave in front of his girlfriend’s half-naked family. Dismukes’s character, who is fully clothed and ostensibly normal, is immediately othered and unnerved, constantly humiliating himself in front of a be-lingeried family who are nothing but welcoming.
Bensinger came up in the Chicago improv and sketch-comedy scene, where he met future collaborators including Sarah Sherman, Conner O’Malley, and his Joy Tactics podcast co-hosts Nate Varrone and Eric Rahill. Just as O’Malley and Rahill’s work is infatuated with toxic masculinity and fratty hopecore, Bensinger’s is obsessed with sheepish dude-empaths hiding beneath layers of uneasy bravado. In the film Rap World (which Bensinger also edited), Bensinger, O’Malley, and Rahill play suburban deadbeats eager to make an album, each man waylaid by his own hubris and distractions. Bensinger’s character, Casey, talks tough — “I’m a superhero and I only kill teachers,” he freestyles at one point — but is adrift and lonely. He sparks to life only when chatting up a random girl (Sherman) the group encounters in a grocery-store parking lot. “We both have, uh, hoodies on!” he says as he stumbles through a pickup line, his deadpan sincerity grounding the film’s comedy in something more tangibly humane.
After moving to New York in 2018, Bensinger began to home in on stand-up and self-produced sketches as his dominant forms, the latter of which have steadily grown into more ambitious shorts. They tend to focus on troubled outsiders searching for some kind of fulfillment in a world that won’t indulge it. In “Peripheral,” which functions like a parody of a CW show, Bensinger plays Julian, a man who suffers from “peripheral vision syndrome” due to a welding mishap, which complicates his will-they-won’t-they relationship with a girl (Blue Heron’s Amy Zimmer). Bensinger’s deft physical comedy keeps “Peripheral” light despite the sketch’s tragic core. (Julian’s condition forces him to lumber around at a diagonal angle so he can see where he’s going.) Sure, his characters could catch a break once in a while, but where’s the fun in that?
  
  
    .
    Two Quick Questions With Jack
    
  At this point in your comedy career, is there someone you’ve proved demonstrably wrong? If so, whom and how?
I tried doing improv in Chicago for many years before realizing stand-up is a better fit, and one time I had an improv coach tell me I should be myself less. I don’t fault them, because I was a nuisance to do improv with. I was doing written stand-up jokes in scenes and had a catchphrase. I was soaking wet one time, which was not cool. I was using my phone to Google things during scenes. Eventually I realized I should just quit, even though it was all in good fun, and find some fellow weirdos who liked when I would mess with them. But yeah, that person who said to stop being myself — I disagree, probably, in a sense.
When you think about the future of comedy, what concerns you, and what excites you?
I think what we can all very much look forward to is the collapse of the comedy industry. Then anybody who wants to make comedy can move to a suburb of Virginia Beach where the rent is a little lower, then when all the money and celebrity stuff is gone, it’ll just be people making stuff because they had a funny idea, and not because they want to eventually start their own probiotic NA beer or sexual liquor company.
Dukes
Even if you haven’t heard of Dukes before, chances are you’re familiar with its two stars or at least have come across their work online. SNL cast member Jane Wickline is best known for her “Weekend Update” guest pieces in which she often sings songs that push her naturally awkward sensibility to the extreme, like a 2024 segment where she tells a story about overstaying her welcome at a party so long that the police show up. Liva Pierce first went viral during college in 2019 for a masterful yet slapdash front-facing comedy video demonstrating what it’s like when musicals switch from speaking to singing. Dukes, named because dykes + dudes = dukes, is the result of these two codependent Gen-Zers combining their powers. In their self-titled show, which played Soho Playhouse in New York this summer, they performed in baggy button-downs with teenage-boy-still-growing-into-his-limbs physicality and casual ease that belie hard-hitting punch lines. In one song, Pierce impersonates themself as a teen whose attempt to seduce the mom of a child they’re babysitting gets sidetracked by the mom taking too keen an interest in their androgyny: “No! MILF, no!” they sing in a staccato shout. “Don’t question your gender right now!”
Pierce grew up in Maine and founded their high school’s first improv troupe before attending the University of Chicago, where they performed in the school’s improv troupe (alongside 2025 Comedian You Should Know Jo Sunday) and studied at Second City. Wickline, meanwhile, has comedy in her blood; her father was an original staff writer on Late Night With David Letterman. She joined Oberlin’s sketch group during college and initially blew up on TikTok for off-kilter sketches playing people happily oblivious to the way the world works. In one 2021 sketch that currently has more than 6 million views, she’s a flight passenger who thinks that the “call flight attendant” button is a restroom button that will turn her seat into a bathroom.
After graduating in 2021 and 2022, respectively, Wickline and Pierce moved to New York and met while performing at open mics in the city. During a shared 35-minute bus ride after one of those mics in Williamsburg, they struck up a friendship and comedy collaboration, which began with a video about how adult friendships are so difficult to make that a “Bureau of Friendship” has to govern the process. Individually, they’re experts at lampooning Gen-Z self-consciousness from the inside; together, their tight friendship is clumsily aspirational.
  
  
    .
    Three Quick Questions With Dukes
    
  What’s the biggest financial investment you’ve made for your comedy, and how were you able to afford it? 
Jane: Our ill-advised Off Broadway show is a complete financial disaster. We invested in ourselves by paying for production costs with our tour earnings. We are recouping our losses with the currency of fun.
If you taught a comedy class, what’s the most crucial lesson you’d want your students to learn?
Liva: I took a lot of comedy classes as a young adult in an openly careerist way. I really wanted someone to tell me how to get famous. If I taught a class now, I would try to weed out anyone who is sick like I was and kindly tell them that their goals are bad and that they need to first figure out a way to enjoy toiling in obscurity for forever. My solution has been to try to write and work with people I think are (1) geniuses,( 2) kind, (3) available to hang out. After that, I just kind of try to keep up with them, which is quite enjoyable. All that said, I hope I never have to teach a class on comedy. I don’t know a thing.
What’s the most earnest goal you have?
Jane: To write earnest music. I would love to write a (non-comedy) musical.
Liva: I want my work to be so undeniable and big that I get to throw my phone in the garbage. There’s sometimes a reductive narrative about young comedians, or honestly just young artists, that’s like, “These ‘digital natives’ can’t get enough of the internet! Yummy internet! Their phone is their paintbrush and their canvas!” Maybe this is because I am at the older end of Gen Z, but it’s the opposite for me and most of my friends. Many of us feel forced to make content online because we’re trying to keep up with broader, often corporation-driven trends around media monetization and the evolution of digital marketing. I would love to never have to post about the things I am writing or performing ever again. It’s a tremendous time suck.
Grace Johnson
Grace Johnson went from being a corporate lawyer to saying stuff like “Ketanji Brown Jackson should be getting her ass ate right now” to rooms full of people. Born in Nigeria and raised in New York, Johnson was working in data law when the pandemic hit and she stumbled into comedy on Clubhouse, the audio-only chatting app that thrived during lockdown. When restrictions began to lift in 2021, she started hitting open mics before confusing her immigrant single mother by leaving law to pursue comedy. The legal system’s loss turned out to be comedy’s gain.
Johnson is a consummate natural, sheathing her type-A personality in R-rated humor and a laid-back, comfortable demeanor. She assembles jokes like layer cakes, alternating between personal and universal, political activism and pure chill. In what begins as a normal-enough setup for a joke about dating apps, Johnson says she matched on Hinge with someone whose profile says, “I did crack once.” This prompts a whole tangent about “throat goat” Nancy Reagan and how “economics wasn’t the only thing that was trickling down, baby,” which then builds to a surprising pinch of attachment-style humor: “Nancy said, ‘Just say no,’ ’cause crack is addictive … I got trust issues, okay? ’Cause if you couldn’t commit to crack, how you gonna commit to me?”
In 2022, Johnson worked as a writing consultant on the Canadian short-form comedy series virgins! and founded Pink Lotion Comedy, a pop-up show for Black female and nonbinary comics. In 2025 she was named one of Just for Laughs’ New Faces. Beyond her honed material, Johnson is a prolific riffer. On Instagram and TikTok, she can rant for minutes on end about whatever headline or trending topic she comes across, from something as goofy as linking big booties to neurodivergence via Australia’s lack of both to more pressing news like how AI data centers’ freshwater depletion will lead to even less ass-washing among the general population than there already is. She also riffs well with others, making her the best possible co-host on any comedy lineup in New York, especially on her monthly Union Hall show, Crank That, with Niles Abston and Zae Jordan. In November, she’ll headline her own show, an “evening of comedy & ADHD tangents,” at the New York Comedy Festival.
  
  
    .
    Two Quick Questions With Grace
    
  When you think about the future of comedy, what concerns you, and what excites you?
Excites: Seeing kind people win. Watching the show Funny AF and seeing people I know and respect be successful. Seeing Black women and NB peeps have fun onstage. Seeing genuine oddballs find their audiences. Josh Johnson’s newer style being embraced. Audiences getting curious about comedy again and going outside to laugh together. “Having taste” is making an important resurgence. New live-show formats. Black people doing improv.
Concerns: People chasing laughs and relatability until they lose their point of view. That’s the fastest way to get bottom-barrel thoughts, milquetoasty art, and watered-down everything. Stand-up is similar to a guided tour at a museum: You’re supposed to bring the audience into your world of curated experiences, then show them what to look at and how you want them to look at it. There’s nothing new under the sun, but at least show them something old in a new way. They’re free to derive their own meaning once you’re done, but try!
What’s the most earnest goal you have?
To retire my mom, refurbish the school in my village named after my grandfather, pay off the student loans of me and everyone I love, and make Queen Latifah proud of me.
Hayden Johnson
In her early years as a stand-up, Hayden Johnson performed a lot of material about people’s perception of her as a trans woman. “I hope that people see me as a girl,” she recalled thinking during those years on Caleb Hearon’s podcast So True. But since moving to L.A. in 2021 after starting comedy in Athens, Ohio, in 2018, her disposition has grown more absurdist and far less apologetic. In one 2025 TikTok video, she addresses people who insist on pointing out they can see her Adam’s apple. “Don’t worry because I’m going to get surgery,” she innocently responds before abruptly shifting into a guttural rage, “to make it huge! I’m going to have a neck like a frog — just giant every time I talk! You won’t have to worry about how deep my voice is for long, because pretty soon I’m just going to be going, ‘Ribbit! Ribbit!’” Johnson’s identity also comes with a list of assumptions about her politics, and she has fun playing with those too. “I like trans porn,” she begins in a joke from earlier this year. “The only part of trans porn that I don’t like is that part in the middle where they both stop having sex, turn to the camera, and repeat, ‘Assassinate Charlie Kirk,’ for 20 minutes.”
Johnson is best known for co-creating the live show Trans-It Girls alongside fellow trans comedian (and former Comedian You Should Know) Nori Reed, which has attracted an impressive list of guest performers including John Early, Hannah Einbinder, and Mae Martin. She was selected as a Just for Laughs New Face in 2025 and is currently touring her debut hour of stand-up, the not-so-understatedly titled Piss Queen. One of her tour stops was a recent headlining slot at the Netflix Is a Joke festival, where she began her set with a statement she says her representatives asked her to read to be brand-friendly. “Boy, oh boy, do I love Netflix, a perfect company that’s never done anything wrong,” she reads off her phone with a mischievous grin. She then lists a series of acts that “a lot of woke gay comedians” would be upset to share a festival bill with, including Louis C.K., “Tires the show,” Tony Hinchcliffe, “vaguely Saudi Arabia,” and Jerry Seinfeld. “I love that Jerry Seinfeld dated a 17-year-old girl when he was a 38-year-old man,” she continues. “I think people should stop bringing it up.”
  
  
    .
    Two Quick Questions With Hayden
    
  At this point in your comedy career, is there someone you’ve proved demonstrably wrong? If so, whom and how?
I’m pretty sure every time I’ve been in a classic comedy-club greenroom, the other comics are assuming I’m just there to blow one of the headliners. It’s nice to be an underdog — for boys to think I’m a diversity hire and then to kill harder than they ever will in their life. Nothing beats the feeling of watching some hack douchebag bomb, going onstage after him, bullying him, crushing so hard they let me do another ten, coming offstage, and blowing the headliner.
What’s the biggest financial investment you’ve made for your comedy, and how were you able to afford it?
Moving to Los Angeles from Ohio. I was working at the Starbucks at USC (I was not a student, which I feel compelled to say). Then I’d get off work, do DoorDash, and go to open mics. I built up a lot of credit-card debt trying to make it all work. It’s worth being poor to do comedy, though. It’s like being an old-timey painter, except no one will respect me when I’m dead.
Li Jin Hao
Li Jin Hao tends to deliver his stand-up in a soothing, unhurried coo. With his blend of surrealism, wordplay, and philosophical observation, his performances can feel like an M.F.A. student’s spoken-word recital until he flips his affect, unleashing bursts of aggression and machismo. When he talks in his debut special, Swimming in a Submarine, about his mandatory service in the Singaporean army, for example, he mimes a gun with his fingers and childishly says, “Pew-pew!” Then a terrifying expression overtakes his face as his imaginary gun transforms into an assault rifle, and he acts out mowing down civilians in violent combat: “The first thing they taught us in the army is, ‘You pull the trigger not to hurt what’s in front, but to protect what’s behind,’ which, first of all, is a potato-potahto approach.” Later, there’s another unexpected turn during an otherwise pun-heavy bit about dating a ghost. This apparition, he says, was hard to date because she was “so possessive” and once accused him of cheating on her because he was watching a horror movie. “‘Baby, come on, it just popped up on my screen,’” he tells her. “‘First of all, I see right through you,’” she replies. Li dips into a swaggering bro persona and delivers his punch line (“Which is whatever coming from a ghost!”) directly to a front-row audience member like they’re two guys commiserating about women being hypocrites. “I got you, man,” he repeats, after dapping him up. Then, shifting registers once again, he stares into the audience member’s soul and says, “I have you.”
After completing his military service in 2019, Li began performing open mics in Singapore before moving to Scotland the same year to study English and film at the University of St. Andrews, where he continued developing his comedy by joining the school’s sketch-comedy revue. After graduating in 2023, he moved to London, where he continued to develop his act and reached the finals of the BBC New Comedy Awards. The following year, he took Swimming in a Submarine to the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, where he scored a nomination for Best Newcomer. This distinction unlocked a series of mainstream opportunities for the comedian, who has since performed on Comedy Central U.K.’s Comedy Central Live, wrote and acted on the sketch show Mitchell and Webb Are Not Helping, and most notably landed a role in the upcoming Judd Apatow and Glen Powell movie, The Comeback King. In August, his second solo show, Falling From a Moon, netted him an even more prestigious nomination for Best Comedy Show at Edinburgh. The show’s official description, par for the course for Li, is less of an indication of the show’s content than a series of non sequiturs. “Remember Pangea?” it asks. “It was the first Brexit.”
  
  
    .
    Two Quick Questions With Jin Hao
    
  What’s the biggest financial investment you’ve made for your comedy, and how were you able to afford it? 
When I started, my mom and stepdad rented out my room back home in Singapore to help me. They lived with strangers so I could do the Edinburgh Fringe festival. But now that things are stable, they still live with them. Perhaps they are no longer strangers. Maybe they are their new son.
When you think about the future of comedy, what concerns you, and what excites you? 
I’m super-excited that new subgenres of comedy are emerging, and from what I see it’s no longer a simple binary of traditional versus alternative. I think of comedians as animals in a zoo, and it concerns me when the owl looks at the lion with jealousy and tries to imitate its growls without realising that their speciality is staying up at night and being able to turn their head fully. It worries me when an artist measures their success using someone else’s ruler. I worry they compromise their voice for this. I’m really sad that I’ve come to the end of the questions.
Ania Magliano
From having to deliver the first-ever “Weekend Update” joke on SNL U.K. earlier this year to occupying the archetypal Young Person Slot™ on Taskmaster in 2025, Ania Magliano often finds herself succeeding in high-pressure comedic situations by being a little stinker. The latter role, a placement often granted to recent Edinburgh Festival Fringe graduates with promising futures, saw Magliano devise a delightful solution to deal with her fellow contestants picking on her as a representative of her whole generation: She went full baby. The Cambridge Footlights alum and Chicken Shop Date writer staunchly maintained that she was host and titular Taskmaster Greg Davies’s long-lost daughter, going as far as to fake a paternity test in the finale. She’s a bisexual Bugs Bunny or Dennis the Menace with a knack for petulance and lateral thinking that also serve her well on SNL U.K., where alongside co-anchor Paddy Young, she reacts to doomful headlines with a coquettish eyebrow raise and delivers the segment’s edgiest lines in the driest tone possible. Consider that opening joke: “Coming up on tonight’s ‘Weekend Update’: pedophilia. But first: war!” she begins with an impish smile. “Yesterday, in a shock U-turn, Keir Starmer finally gave his consent for President Trump to use British bases to protect the Strait of Hormuz, at which point Trump said, ‘Consent? Now you’ve taken all the fun out of it!’”
As a stand-up, Magliano paints herself as a charming neurotic addicted to the internet. When unpacking why an ex once called her a prude, she couches her dislike of morning sex as something people shouldn’t do “whilst the blackbird is singing his morning tune.” (That she gives the word tune a slightly distinctive English ch– skewers her own Cambridge background.) Magliano sold out the recent Edinburgh Festival Fringe run of her stand-up show Peach Fuzz four years after her first time at the festival, and her first U.S. shows this December keep selling out, proving she doesn’t need a panel show or ensemble to pull a crowd. Her charm offensive translates across the pond.
  
  
    .
    Two Quick Questions With Ania
    
  At this point in your comedy career, is there someone you’ve proved demonstrably wrong? If so, whom and how?
My boyfriend when I was 15 was really into stand-up and got me into it. He showed me a lot of American comics I hadn’t come across before. He wanted to be a comedian and once said to me, half joking, “I hope you never try stand-up, because you’ll be better than me at it.” So you could chalk my whole career up to spite. I guess I haven’t proved him wrong, though. No, I wish him well — he’s happily married with a wife and kids. Shout-out!
If you taught a comedy class, what’s the most crucial lesson you’d want your students to learn?
Probably to home in on the stuff that feels really weird and specific and say that. Of course everyone wants to be a comedian these days because it’s rock and roll, but I think that means audiences see and hear the same things over and over and over. I think you can tell on some deep intuitive level when a comic is saying something they actually mean and is true to them, and while it can be more vulnerable to try to do that, the payoff of connecting with an audience that way is pretty special.
Janet McNamara
In Janet McNamara’s 2026 YouTube special Not Smart Enough, her first special, she describes the experience of trying to get an autism diagnosis. It’s a defining part of her story: In an episode of This American Life in August, McNamara details years of wondering why she can’t perform the social niceties other people handle with ease, which has made her day job as an accountant increasingly difficult. She goes to a neuropsychologist for an evaluation, hoping to finally get accommodations at her workplace, and, after hours of testing, the doctor breaks the news to her. “He looked at me right in the eye — which I did not care for,” McNamara recalls, pausing for the audience to react. Finally, his expert medical opinion: “‘You are so close.’” That joke, which McNamara hits with a palpable sparkle of smugness, illustrates how deliciously blunt her comedic sensibility is. Her unusual brain is often the subject of her material, but she understands how to be inside and outside the world of the joke at the same time, making her a thrilling narrator of her own perspective.
McNamara’s first experience with fame was in 2010, when she filmed a deliberately cringe-inducing audition for American Idol that went megaviral. Sixteen years later, that performance of a woman clueless about her own awkwardness has morphed into McNamara’s more settled, self-possessed stage persona, sharpened by years of stand-up in her hometown of Boston and more recently at the Comedy Cellar in New York. She has not transformed into someone who appears relaxed and casual onstage; she still holds herself stiffly, often wearing an oddly fitting puffer vest, and delivers her jokes in a desert-dry deadpan. But she is more controlled and commanding than she was during that American Idol phase. “I used to be hot … Being hot is stupid,” one of her jokes goes. “Last year was the best year of my life. I gained 40 pounds last year, I got a promotion, Bill Burr follows me, and now I don’t get cold.” McNamara is right: The best iteration of her is the one who flaunts all the things that make her most herself.

    Two Quick Questions With Janet
    
  What non-comedy skill do you possess that you’re most proud of?
I had a full-time job as an accountant up until a few months ago. I didn’t bullshit my day job as an accountant; I was good at it and worked hard. Creating templates, best practices, and workflows was my first passion. Audits are fun — at least they are when they don’t find anything.

I’d like to be able to complete a 500-piece jigsaw puzzle in less than an hour. Right now, it takes me about four hours, but I’ve been studying professional puzzlers on YouTube, and I think with the right focus I can make it happen by 2030.
Courtney O’Donnell
“Hi, I’m Chanty Beluga!” With these four words, Courtney O’Donnell gave zillennials a brain-rot character to call their own, a dash of midsummer Dada to amuse people getting nothing done on their computers. In the weeks after the comedian first posted a short video of her oddly named, swordfish-burrito-ordering alter ego to Instagram on July 28, she inspired a soundalike contest, received press coverage and brand deals, and in a true mark of virality, a celebrity (Gwyneth Paltrow) attempted to hide behind Chanty’s goodwill to curb a PR crisis. Although it may seem like Chanty apparated on our feeds one day out of thin air cold foam, she’s really an emissary from the strange land of Planet Courtney.
Until 2024, O’Donnell worked in social-media marketing, running socials for McDonald’s during the Great Grimace Mass Hysteria of 2023. She is fluent in the language of microinfluencers, clout chasers, and how branded content infiltrates every aspect of our online existence. She channels this knowledge of the wannabe-girlboss backrooms of Instagram Reels into satire that is just loopy enough to distract from how sharp it cuts. O’Donnell’s characters are usually fresh out of divorces and staying afloat on waves of delusional self-confidence and optimism. In one video from January 2026, she dances in a body-con dress under the caption, “Who said a mother of three with treatment-resistant IBS can’t blow off some steam at the Annual Orlando Salesforce Summit.” Some of her other characters are more obliviously nefarious, like the one who smirks over a caption, saying, “Just invested $150,000 in Palantier and now I’m going to get mochi pancakes with my sister-in-law. Life gets better.”
Alongside comedian Chelsea Morgan, O’Donnell posts “clip-farmed” videos from a fake podcast called Yep! She Went There, where their pseudoscientific chatter is like Conner O’Malley for a MAHA-susceptible girliepop-ulation. All of these elements are at work in her one-woman live show Planet Courtney, where she plays a resident of the titular planet where the hospital is run by Chipotle, the Air Force is controlled by Aritzia, and “the Sprinkles cupcake ATM downtown is now taking ancient Sumerian shekels.” It’s Barbie’s world from Barbie, if Barbie’s world was completely taken over by GLP-1-friendly slop bowls and VC-backed DTC brands. It’s exhausting but breathtaking to witness the amount of world-building and referential jokes O’Donnell packs in when she’s just doing a 15-minute shred of her full act on a group show.

    Two Quick Questions With Courtney
    
  If you taught a comedy class, what’s the most crucial lesson you’d want your students to learn?
Do things that feel fun to you, not what you think is going to be funny. A friend of mine recently gave me such a nice compliment. Milan Patel
Sometimes a joke is more powerful when it forces an audience to slow down. Milan Patel’s comedy works best that way. He’s most potent onstage when he deliberately pumps the brakes, interrupts the rhythm of a joke, and pushes his audience to stop and stare at him. The opening joke from his 2026 Don’t Tell Comedy set is the clearest expression of that impulse. Patel says he quit using ChatGPT after learning about how much water it takes for the AI to answer a single query. “If ChatGPT was a human being and it did that, we would be so pissed off,” he argues. “I was just wondering, Are chia seeds good for me?” he imagines asking. He then pauses, puts the microphone back in the stand, and chugs an entire bottle of water before answering: “Yeah, they’re pretty good for you.”
Raised in the Pacific Northwest and now based in L.A., Patel has been developing his act as an opener at Largo, and he now tours his variety show Milan Patel & the Enemies of My Enemies, which played at the 2026 Netflix Is a Joke Fest. That show includes animation and sketches as well as absurdist act-outs and character portraits, like Patel’s parody of one-man shows. (Patel’s character work has also led to his move into acting, including a one-off role in season two of Peacock’s The Paper.) In all of those examples of his work, Patel’s strength is in allowing the audience to sit for just a moment before the punch line arrives. His 2025 Netflix Introducing … showcase set closes with a pitch for a nightmare video-game-like dating app that gains more momentum with each line, turning into a runaway train of features like “berserker mode” and shields to prevent being rejected. But that joke is built on the rhythm he’s established earlier in the set, where he plays a hippie meteorologist responsible for determining the “feels like” temperature. There’s nothing more mundane than a joke about the weather, but Patel ekes every ounce of humor out of the gap inside of “high of 63, but it feels … like 65.”

    One Quick Question With Milan
    
  What non-comedy skill do you possess that you’re most proud of?
I can scream really loud, but only when I’m scared. The trick is to relax your anus and open your mouth really wide. It essentially creates a wind tunnel from your ass to your esophagus. This can be really useful if I see a big rat in a restaurant. It both alerts the other guests and focuses a bunch of attention on me, which I love. I’ve tried using my screaming ability onstage, but most of the venues don’t have rats, so I have to release my own. My goal is to be in a Godzilla movie.
Hassan Phills
When people stumble across memes about the Toronto accent on social media, they’re usually seeing a Malibu’s Most Wanted version of it that has gone through several layers of context collapse. Watching Hassan Phills’s stand-up is an exercise in restoring the lost nuance. From the slang he uses to his inclination to double over laughing at so-bad-they’re-good pick-up lines, Phills is an unabashed Toronto Man. He’s even friendly with Drake, who featured a snippet of one of Phills’s TikTok videos on his song “Small Town Fame” in 2025. But more than that, he’s a reflection of the city’s complicated pluralism: a half-Jamaican, half-Somali Muslim who grew up in a neighborhood full of Desis, all of which finds its way into his stand-up. Sometimes, all this diversity is mesmerizing; in one joke, he talks about hanging out in a notorious Greater Toronto Area plaza where you’re liable to see “hijabis doing doughnuts in the parking lot” and hear “bare bhangra” playing at 2 a.m. Other times, he examines how it produces new layers of racism. Back when he worked retail, he had a manager named “Amanda” who gave him shit for sporting an Afro on the job, he begins another joke. The twist? She was actually an Indian lady named Amandeep. “What’s wrong with this POC double agent?” he asks. “I miss when racism was exclusive. Now it’s all-inclusive, like a resort.”
Phills’s stand-up journey began in Vancouver, where he moved to play collegiate basketball at Capilano University in 2013. In 2015, a manager he worked with at Foot Locker (not Amandeep) signed him up for a local open mic. After a couple years of trying to juggle basketball practice with open mics, Phills decided to throw himself fully into comedy. He moved back to Toronto in 2020 and built a following on social media with silly front-facing videos, which led to higher-profile opportunities. He’s played Hassan, a character loosely based on himself in the Crave original sitcom The Office Movers since 2024; been featured on large platforms like Don’t Tell Comedy and Subway Takes; and was selected as a Just for Laughs New Face this year.
Building a diverse audience in Toronto has naturally translated to global appeal. Phills has traveled everywhere from Nairobi to New York’s Gramercy Theatre to Canada’s Northwest Territories to perform shows; dates in London, Paris, Copenhagen, and Oslo are still to come. But even when he’s literally in the Arctic Circle, he’s committed to “reverse the stigma” on Toronto slang. “Tings,” he jokes in one video, is merely an acronym for “Talented Individuals Navigating Greatness Successfully.” You can almost hear a Toronto woman kissing her teeth then smiling begrudgingly.

    Two Quick Questions With Hassan
    
  What non-comedy skill do you possess that you’re most proud of?
While I’m not the strongest in certain aspects of business or particular technical skills, I have self-awareness that has led me to have the right people around me. I care about people and community, and that care is reflected in how they show up for me. When I was doing my earliest shows, friends and community groups would do everything from handling tickets and chairs to helping sell my merch. My career has been supported by the people who believed in me but didn’t need to.
What’s the most earnest goal you have?
To put myself in a position where I can benefit my family, my friends, and members of my community. I come from a tough neighborhood in Teesdale, Toronto, without much. Basketball allowed me to make it out, and comedy has continued to be my saving grace. I’m able to materially impact the lives of the people I care about the most, and there is no greater joy to me than knowing I can.
I want to continue to travel the world with the people I care about, learning about different cultures and communities, and sharing experiences in different area codes, because life is a lot more enjoyable when you have your people next to you. Being able to be at a dinner or playing Catan in a new city with my peopledem — that is what I strive for. On a professional end, it’s to continue becoming the best comedian I can be, to elevate my game in every respect, and keep developing my pen and learning from the people in the rooms I am now a part of.
Taneshia “Just Nesh” Rice
It’s fitting that Taneshia Rice goes by the stage name Just Nesh, because she has a way of getting straight to the point. “Fuck Katt Williams,” she begins her first hourlong special, Self Served. (She’s not beefing with the comedian, she explains. She’s just trying to get on Club Shay Shay.) Soon after, she’s expressing annoyance with bullshit euphemisms for “fat,” such as “plus-sized” and “heavy set,” the latter of which makes it sound “like you need a dolly” to move her. She cuts through the pro-choice versus pro-life debate with one line: “I’m pro–who the fuck gon’ take care of this baby?” But her material is also full of well-disguised turns and delivered with such precise timing that, even when performing without an audience, as she does on her 2017 album Mixing Vodka With Emotions, she sticks the landing on every note. In one standout joke on Self Served, she discusses how pharmacies lock up the Plan B pill so it’s impossible to buy them in quiet dignity. You have to ring a bell to summon an employee, she explains. “It be like, ‘Ding, aisle three. Bitch got nutted in.’” When they finally come to open the case, she continues, they’re carrying “sparklers like bottle girls.”
All of this is a function of Nesh’s tireless work as a road comic, which she’s been able to pursue, she explains in Self Served, because her mom helps take care of her son, who’s now 18. Her sacrifices have not been in vain; she’s found a champion in Kevin Hart, who featured her on his Comedy Central stand-up showcases Hart of the City in 2016 and The Next Level in 2017 and will release her Hulu half-hour special as part of his LOL Live series in October. Since 2023, she’s also written for BET+’s The Ms. Pat Show, an experience that informs the incredible closing joke on Self Served. While staying with a friend in Atlanta, where the show’s production takes place, she fell into a routine of dropping her friend’s son off at school, which caused her to feel guilty for “cheating” on her son. It’s a joke that only Nesh could write, inspired by experiences wholly unique to her. “I started making him late ’cause you not finna have better attendance than my son,” she says jokingly. To spoil more of the joke’s punch lines would be criminal, but rest assured her son eventually confronts her about it. Not tolerating nonsense apparently runs in the family.

    Two Quick Questions With Just Nesh
    
  If you taught a comedy class, what’s the most crucial lesson you’d want your students to learn?
Don’t be afraid of silence. As comedians, we’re always chasing the big laugh, but there’s power in the quiet moments too. Silence can mean the audience is listening, thinking, or even learning something new. It means you have their undivided attention, and that’s powerful. Every second onstage doesn’t have to be filled with laughter to be effective. Sometimes the quiet is what makes the next laugh hit even harder.
What’s the most earnest goal you have?
To travel the world selling out theaters doing stand-up. That’s the dream for me. Of course, I want to do movies and television and continue creating in other spaces, but ultimately, I want those opportunities to lead more people back to my comedy. I want to build an audience that will come see me live in theaters across the country and eventually around the world. At the end of the day, I just want to be onstage making people laugh — just on a much, much bigger scale.
Ethan Simmons-Patterson
If his stand-up material is to be believed, Ethan Simmons-Patterson’s life in New York City, where he’s lived since 2015, is a constant stream of improbable experiences. He’s being asked by unhoused people whether he’s “got any sandwiches,” getting romantic advice from a racist cop while he has his gun pointed at him, and having a run-in with an environmentally conscious “crackhead” on the street. (“Can’t smoke crack in a world that doesn’t exist,” the “crackhead” tells Simmons-Patterson after carefully disposing his glass crack pipe in the recycling bin.) Whether these stories are fictional or heightened for comic effect is irrelevant; Simmons-Patterson’s conversational delivery and sly smile are so magnetic that audiences want to spend time in his universe either way. The same goes for his perspectives on race, dating, gender, and generational divides shaped by his upbringing in Waukegan, Illinois. Even at his most contrarian, his material never feels alienating. “We got to stop letting Gen X and baby boomers pretend like they didn’t make us who we are,” he says in one joke. “Y’all looked us in our eyes when we were kids, and y’all were like, ‘You could be whatever you want to be as long as you put your mind to it. You can do whatever you want to do.’ And then we grew up and we were like, ‘I want to be a woman,’ and they were like ‘What the fuck?!’ And we were like, ‘No, I’m calling your bluff, dude.’”
It’s the type of material that would play well on social media, if Simmons-Patterson had any interest in playing the followers game. His online presence consists solely of a sparingly used Instagram account created and run by his friends. He rarely tours, appears on podcasts, or engages in any sort of self-promotion. After starting comedy at 18 in college in Iowa City, he moved to New York to strengthen his chops as a comedian, and this one-track approach has paid dividends. He regularly performs at the Comedy Cellar, and he’s landed a number of prestigious opportunities thanks to his reputation for being a killer onstage. He’s performed on Comedy Central’s Stand-Up Featuring and This Week at the Comedy Cellar, was selected as a Just for Laughs New Face in 2022, and was named on Netflix’s newly launched The Shortlist earlier this year. He navigates the industry, just like he does his craft, by inviting people to meet him where he is as opposed to vice versa.
Two Quick Questions With Ethan
What’s the biggest financial investment you’ve made for your comedy, and how were you able to afford it?
Having a separate job as a nurse to be able to live a semi-normal life and pull jokes from a place of exploring my environment — not living life to mine bits, but trying to enjoy life to the point where I still love stand-up and writing. I think the biggest investment you can make in your stand-up is trying to make sure, financially, you can do simple stuff like go on dates, go to the movies, the beach, a concert, etc., which I think is getting harder for people from working-class backgrounds or poorer backgrounds, especially in New York. And just to make sure you get a job, if you can, and work that job, even if you feel like it’s taking away from the comedy. It will come back to you tenfold in your happiness and hopefully allow you to enjoy life. Preachy, I know. Sorry.
When you think about the future of comedy, what concerns you, and what excites you?
What concerns me about comedy is people from richer backgrounds flooding the scene and being able to outlast people from humble backgrounds, then the voice of comedy kind of becoming this fake thing that’s based not on merit but on how long you can survive pursuing it. Also, I’m afraid of people with established careers in something else pivoting to stand-up comedy for another revenue stream and weakening the art form.
I’m excited about the new voices that are coming out — the younger generations that have to fight through social media and all the news we have and AI. There is so much to talk about now, and there’s nuance. Comics can be so many things all at once now, and that lends itself to new jokes that play with old stereotypes and also with new stereotypes that we’ve never heard of. I’m excited people still love to show up and sit still for new voices, whether they know them or not. I think the future is bright for stand-up, especially if we try to make it more accessible to people who love it and want to be great at it.
Ron Taylor
Great comedy chops aren’t built overnight, and although Ron Taylor’s comedy career was shot out of a cannon after winning Kevin Hart’s Netflix stand-up reality show Funny AF in May, his recent success is the result of a decade spent building his style and point of view. After earning a little money from stand-up in his hometown of Detroit in the early 2010s, Taylor bought a van, drove to L.A., and spent the next several years living in that van, working odd jobs, and writing stand-up material. He worked as a doorman at the Comedy Store and filmed videos where he invited his friends over for van-cooked meals, and, in the process, he developed what has become his signature style of cheerful vintage suaveness that is laconic but not withholding. In jokes like his standout bit on Black Oscar-winning movies, or on the absurdity of 21 as the legal drinking age, he lays out a straightforward premise then keeps pulling and pulling on the idea. It’s not just that you can fight for your country before you can legally drink, he says in that joke about being 21. It’s that you can do porn at 18. You can, Taylor notes with some delight, be a taxpaying porn actor coming home at the end of the day and still not be allowed to have a beer: “You’re sticky, you’re crunchy, your pussy’s on fire, you go home to three screaming kids, and you gotta drink a Capri Sun?!”
In 2018, Taylor was voted a Just for Laughs New Face, and in 2024 he released an hourlong special on Veeps called Avalanche, solidifying the sensibility that would make him so appealing on Funny AF. His Afro and leather jacket project swagger, but there’s an appealing openness in his material, too, a willingness to self-deprecate in service of a harder joke. In his Don’t Tell Comedy set from 2022, he talks about a white girlfriend who asked him to try pegging. “I’m sure I’d like it,” he says. “It’s gotta be great. There are marches every June for it.” Taylor has a different concern: “I can’t let a white woman fuck me in the ass!” He won Funny AF with a fantastic run of dick jokes, culminating in his observation that while 12 inches is nearly the size of a Comcast remote, we are now in the streaming era, and Taylor’s working with more of a Roku remote situation. Since Funny AF, he’s appeared on The Tonight Show (performing an airport joke with a miraculously non-hack punch line) and is now touring nationally in preparation for his upcoming Netflix special. He has also, at least according to Kevin Hart, quit his day job scooping ice cream.

    Two Quick Questions With Ron
    
  What non-comedy skill do you possess that you’re most proud of?
I don’t know that I would call it a skill, but I do like to cook. I liked building stuff in high school and had planned to do it in college, but all the math made my head hurt, so I instead went into theater arts to do stand-up. The desire to build things was still there, though. I scratched that itch with cooking and making food. When you build something, you know you did it right when it works properly; in cooking, you know you did it right when it taste good.
If you taught a comedy class, what’s the most crucial lesson you’d want your students to learn?
I would want students to understand timing. Timing is one of the biggest things to me in comedy. Everyone wants to be fast, but most times the big laughs come from coming in at the right time as opposed to coming in quickly. A lot of us comics go too fast and step on laughs or rush to get a line in, not wanting to miss the moment. If you wait and pay attention, the moment will come back, or you can set up the moment again for an even better moment. Also, if you can get 30 minutes of laughs with 15 minutes of jokes, you’re getting your jokes’ worth!
Sureni Weerasekera
“Stay in your lane” is good advice for student drivers but a limiting mandate for comedians who want to appeal to more than niche audiences and podcast fan bases. It doesn’t apply to Sureni Weerasekera, who has earned a reputation for crushing everywhere from her home base in Brooklyn, to touring college campuses, to the writers’ room on Brittany Broski’s Royal Court, to Netflix’s Introducing … series. The Sri Lanka–born, San Diego–raised 28-year-old UC Berkeley dropout bends her generation’s activist streak inside out and roasts from a place of familiarity. In a bit about sleeping with a Black lesbian cop, which she compares to “fucking a Native American real-estate agent,” she dials up the shock value, saying, “You posted a black square? I fucked a Black box.” Much of her material centers on the child-of-immigrants experience, and it’s in those jokes, based in memories of a vulnerable and complex dynamic in her upbringing, that she lands on emotional truths, like making a crack about how “all immigrant kids are paralegals” tasked with completing paperwork for their parents: “My mom’s like, ‘What’s a dependent?’ I’m like, ‘You, bitch!’”
Weerasekera has a lot of audacity packed into her tiny frame and tends to punctuate her racier jokes with a relaxed, SoCal stoner laugh, kind of like a small bisexual South Asian Gen-Z Seth Rogen. She jokes about all of the usual suspects — sex, dating, being a barista — but her naughty streak leads to fresh takes on the old standards. In her Don’t Tell Comedy set from 2023, she remembers the time she accidentally “chopped off the tip of my finger” while working at a coffee shop, “which is the closest a lesbian can get to a circumcision.” In addition to stand-up, she’s branching out into new media; in 2025, she voiced a cool-girl stoner for Sabrina Brier’s audiobook, That Friend. Earlier this year, she appeared in the indie ensemble piece Human Theories, which made its world premiere at Tribeca.

    Two Quick Questions With Sureni
    
  What’s the most earnest goal you have?
To be the best stand-up comedian, actor, and writer I can be while maintaining freedom, autonomy, and balance. To make my people proud, to put Sri Lankan and Eelam Tamil people on the map, to make my immigrant parents’ sacrifices worth it, to show queer brown girls what curating a life for you can look like. Oh, also to make more money than my project-manager brother. .
At this point in your comedy career, is there someone you’ve proved demonstrably wrong? If so, whom and how?
The racist, sexist, and homophobic people on Facebook Reels who leave comments where they’re like, “this monkey dyke isn’t funny. honey, don’t quit your day job” and I’m like, I wish I had one to quit. I uploaded this clip with Wi-Fi I paid for with these jokes. And every time you comment and engage with my comedy, that’s making my router connection stronger.
Lou Wilson
Between his boisterous laugh and reputation for being a fountain of whimsy, Lou Wilson is Dropout’s most lovable staple. To watch him on Game Changer or Dimension 20 is to witness Wilson excel as an improviser’s improviser, one who lands bits that feel expertly crafted despite their spontaneity and knows that sometimes the best thing to do when a bit tanks is to lean in. But he doesn’t just conjure something from nothing; Wilson’s comedy is both referential and reverential, and every joke is a dip into his well of pop-culture bona fides. When asked to propose visual effects on the spot during an episode of Game Changer, for example, he borrows from the split-screen stylization used in heist films like Ocean’s 11, directing the postproduction team to insert a “little Steven Soderbergh box” of him drifting and flying onto the screen with frantic enthusiasm. For a game in another episode in which the contestants compete to see who can get the “silliest vanity license plate,” he changed his car’s plate to read “IMDAJKR.” But lest anyone misread this as “I’m the jacker,” he also covered his car in a Joker-themed wrap. His commitment to the bit didn’t end there, by the way. He still drives around in this car today.
The Los Angeles native divides his time between multiple Dropout shows and his job as announcer for Jimmy Kimmel Live! A clip of him from the latter went viral last summer, wherein he confronts guest host Nicole Byer about not remembering that they went on a date in 2020, even though the two of them kissed. It’s another example of Wilson wringing a joke from failure by refusing to allow an embarrassing moment slip by without a punch line. “Lou, would you say that was more embarrassing for me or for you?” Byer asks. “For you!” he answers. “How could you forget about a date with me in the year 2020? What else did you have going on, Nicole?” In April, Wilson launched his own live show, Which Wish, in which he urges fellow Dropout pals like Ally Beardsley or Zac Oyama to dream up obscure wishes that he then grants onstage regardless of scale or scope. (He made a giant Wemby puppet for Beardsley and wrote a sample script for Rush Hour 4 for Oyama.) He craves endless opportunities to say “yes, and,” even when he has to invent them himself.
